topics.title: Chapter overview
topics.summary: Optimization preserves the program’s required observable behavior while transforming its implementation. That promise is only meaningful for behavior the language actually defines. A compiler can exploit undefined behavior in ways that make a seemingly harmless source change produce surprising machine code, so correctness and optimization analysis cannot be separated.

topics.title: 14.1.1 Comparing Debug and Optimized Builds
topics.summary: Optimization levels select groups of transformations whose exact contents vary by compiler and release. Debug builds favor convenient inspection; optimized builds favor generated-code quality under the chosen settings. Neither name alone tells you every active option, so retain the actual command line.

topics.title: 14.2.2 Verifying Optimization Assumptions
topics.summary: A comment saying branchless or vectorized is not evidence that the emitted code has that property. Compiler optimization reports and disassembly can support the claim, while a benchmark determines whether the change helps the relevant workload. Both are needed before attributing a speedup to a particular mechanism.

blocks.text: Generated assembly is direct evidence for whether a specific optimization hypothesis, such as inlining or constant folding, occurred in a particular build.

blocks.text: Code or command
rich: Code or command

blocks.text:
g++ -std=c++20 -O0 -S -masm=intel optimize.cpp -o O0.s
g++ -std=c++20 -O3 -S -masm=intel optimize.cpp -o O3.s
diff -u O0.s O3.s | less
blocks.code:
g++ -std=c++20 -O0 -S -masm=intel optimize.cpp -o O0.s
g++ -std=c++20 -O3 -S -masm=intel optimize.cpp -o O3.s
diff -u O0.s O3.s | less

blocks.text: What the important parts do
rich: What the important parts do

blocks.text: `-S` stops after assembly generation and `-masm=intel` selects one readable syntax. Building twice with different optimization levels isolates the compiler policy change; `diff` reveals which calls or calculations disappeared or changed.
